edits.name: Weekly 'what Happy did' text
edits.description: Once a week Tony gets one short text that counts what Happy's tools did for him that week and lists the saved-note files that changed, written by a small script with no model. There is no journal and no 'undo that', and forgetting a conversation stays Tony's command at the Mac. Jordan's copy is a second job of the same kind, about her own agent only.
edits.example: The weekly text, starting with its own label: 'What Happy did this week: web search 9 calls, web helper 3, weather 12, scheduling tool 4. Notes changed: 2 files', followed by the two file names. In a week with nothing to count, no text is sent.
edits.how: One checked-in script, no model and no agent tool. It asks OpenClaw's own activity record for the past week of that parent's agent (`openclaw audit --agent <id> --kind tool_action --status succeeded --after <date> --json`), counts finished calls by tool name, and lists by name the files changed that week in that parent's notes folder (F041). The record is on by default, keeps 30 days and holds no content. The jobs script (G003) creates one command job per parent who gets the text: the owner's handle read from the family file, a time limit, the day and daytime hour Tony names, the text starting with its own label, and `NO_REPLY` when there is nothing to count. The query is tried once from a scheduled command job before the script is written. Not built: a journal table, a copy of note text, an undo tool, a read tool on any agent. House-rules plugin: no rule needed.
depends_on: G003 in its simplified form: the three scheduler switches and the jobs script that creates this job
F041 saved notes, for the 'notes changed' line; until notes exist the text holds the tool counts only
Test first: the activity-record query returns that agent's rows when it is run from a scheduled command job
Tony provides the day and the daytime hour of the weekly text at execution
Tony says at execution whether Jordan's copy (a second job from the same script, about her own agent) is switched on from the start
caveats: Counts are by tool name only: the text says 'scheduling tool 4 calls', not which reminder or list, and a built-in tool that does several things under one name is one line. In-house tools should give each kind of write its own tool name so the counts mean something.
A note file changed twice in one week counts once, and the text shows file names, not what was saved.
There is no 'undo that'. A parent says 'cancel that reminder' or 'change it back to X' and the tool that made the change does it; an item Happy added to a list can be deleted on the phone.
Nothing answers 'what did you do this week?' exactly in mid-week: no agent gets a tool that reads the record.
The activity record keeps 30 days, so the text cannot look further back than that.
Forgetting works per conversation and stays Tony's command at the Mac (`openclaw memory forget`, with `--dry-run` first); nothing is built for it here.
edits.safety: No model and no agent tool are involved. The script reads a record that holds tool names and outcomes but no content, and the file names in one parent's own notes folder. Its one text goes to that parent only, whose handle the jobs script reads from the family file; nothing goes into the other parent's chat.
unverified: That `openclaw audit` can be called from a scheduled command job on the Mac mini and returns one agent's tool rows for the past week; to be tried once before the script is written.

Where saved notes live is settled by F041's own test (T6); that file change times in that folder reflect each save made through the sandbox was not tried.

edits.name: Screen-control pilot on a clean, throwaway virtual Mac (attended by Tony)
edits.description: An experimental pilot: Happy controls the screen of a clean, throwaway virtual Mac that holds no Apple Account, Messages or saved passwords, never Happy's own desktop. It starts with one 'step zero' test and ends there if that fails. If it passes, Tony starts and watches every run of one chore he names at execution; nobody starts a run by text.
edits.example: Step zero: in the throwaway virtual Mac, Happy takes one screenshot and makes one click on an empty desktop while Tony watches. Later Tony starts the chore he named, watches it and reads the result: 'done' or 'stopped: a sign-in window appeared'.
edits.how: Step zero first; if it fails the pilot ends, and no real desktop is ever used. A throwaway macOS guest on the Mac mini (Apple's Virtualization framework, for example the Lume CLI); OpenClaw.app installed in it and paired as its own node; proof that the app runs there without operator rights; one screenshot and one click. For this the MAC-04 entries for `computer.act` and `screen.snapshot` are lifted. If it passes: one `desk` agent with memory off, the minimal tool profile and only `computer` (named in its tool allow and in `tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow`); the guest is reset to a snapshot before every run and may reach only the gateway. Tony starts and watches each run, and stops it with 'Allow Computer Control' in the guest's app or by putting the deny entries back. Test: his chore, run a few times, once with a planted instruction on screen. House-rules plugin: no rule while only Tony starts runs.
depends_on: MAC-04 deny list in place first; its entries for `computer.act` and `screen.snapshot` are lifted for the pilot. The list is Gateway-wide, so no other Mac is paired meanwhile, and if a phone is paired by then its approved command list is re-read first
Tony provides the chore at execution: one family chore that no app or script already handles, with nothing from the never list in it (no payment, purchase, booking, lock or CAPTCHA)
Step zero passes; if it does not, the pilot ends there
Disk and memory on the Mac mini for a macOS guest (OpenClaw's virtual-Mac page asks for about 60 GB of free disk)

A route from the guest to the gateway, which listens on the Mac mini only: the guest's own tailnet identity or an SSH tunnel, limited to the gateway's address and reviewed as a change to the M0 baseline
caveats: The guest is not empty of secrets: the app inside it is signed in to the family gateway. Until step zero shows it running as a device with no operator rights, the agent driving the screen could open a console to everything the clean desk was built to keep away.
Pairing the Mac app pairs a whole device: shell commands, a browser proxy, connector calls and a desktop stream arrive with pointer control. Those stay on the deny list.
There is no check per click and no approval per action: dozens of clicks run unreviewed, so Tony watches every run, and nothing sent by text stops a run in mid-task.

Red-team research on computer-use agents reports injected on-screen instructions succeeding in a large share of attempts, so the tool's built-in warning to the model is a tripwire, not a control. What exists on the controlled desktop is the real boundary.
A desktop that is never reset is the agent's memory: files, open windows and the clipboard carry over from one run to the next.
A pass shows that the chore can be done, not that screen control is safe. Letting anyone start a run by text would need a stop check in code first, as a rule in the house-rules plugin.
edits.safety: The desk agent reads untrusted content (the screen) and holds no memory, accounts or message tool; its ways out are whatever the guest can reach. The trifecta counts as kept only once the app's operator access in the guest is proven absent, the guest reaches only the gateway and it is reset before each run. Never Happy's own desktop; nothing from the never list.

edits.name: Web helper extra readers: a read-only browser for pages that need JavaScript, and text from videos and podcasts
edits.description: The web helper can also read public pages that show nothing without JavaScript, logged out, and pull the text out of videos that have captions and podcasts that publish a transcript, so a parent can ask for the main points from a link. The browser is kept read-only in code: no clicking, typing, form filling or uploads. Bot walls and logins stop it.
edits.example: A parent texts a link to a public page that shows nothing without JavaScript and asks what it says about sign-up dates; the helper opens it in the logged-out browser and the parent's own agent relays the dates with the link. Or Tony texts a link to a long video that has captions and asks for the main points.
edits.how: On the web helper only. (1) Browser: the `browser` tool in the roadmap's sandbox browser container, on its own network with the home network blocked; `sandbox.browser.enabled` for the helper only, `allowHostControl` left false, `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`, the tool named in the helper's tool allow and sandbox tool allow lists. The image is built from a source checkout; if it cannot be built, the browser half is not built, and no host browser is used. (2) House-rules plugin, one rule: for the helper, a short allowlist of read-only browser action names (status, tabs, open, navigate, focus, close, snapshot, text, screenshot); everything else, `act` and `upload` included, is blocked, failing closed. (3) Video and podcast text: a small connector on the Mac mini, allowed to the helper only, wraps `summarize --extract --json` with `--firecrawl off`, no keys and no transcription fallback, and refuses home-network addresses itself. Planted-page cases join the eval suite.

Tony provides at execution: two or three public pages the plain reader returned empty, and a video or podcast link he would want the main points of, as the first test cases

caveats: Bot walls, logins, CAPTCHAs and two-factor prompts stop it. They are reported, never solved, and the docs say sandboxed browser sessions are more likely to be flagged as bots.

The browser image cannot be built from the npm install; it needs a source checkout. There is no fallback to a browser on the Mac itself: if the image cannot be built, only the video and podcast reader ships.

Read-only means no clicking, typing or scrolling, so a page that shows its content only after a click or a scroll stays unreadable. Allowing scrolling or hovering back later needs a further check written then, with an eval case each.
The action names come from the installed 2026.9.7 browser tool and can change with any update. Blocking by default keeps a new action blocked, but the rule needs its test after every OpenClaw update.

The video and podcast reader runs on the Mac mini outside the address checks that cover the page reader and the browser, and it has third-party extraction fallbacks of its own; the wrapper has to switch those off and check the address itself.
A video without captions or a podcast without a published transcript returns nothing: no transcription is set up.
edits.safety: The helper holds no private data, memory or accounts, and the browser profile never holds a login. What a real browser adds is a way to act, so only read-only actions pass, in code that fails closed; page scripts are off and the home network is out of reach.
